nameStory: Micrasterias radiosa doesn't have a widely-used common name, so scientists know it by its scientific name. The genus name 'Micrasterias' comes from Greek words meaning 'small star,' which perfectly describes these tiny, star-shaped algae when viewed under a microscope. The species name 'radiosa' means 'radiating' or 'shining,' referring to how the cell's lobes spread outward like rays of light.
description: Micrasterias radiosa is a single-celled green algae that looks like a microscopic snowflake or star. This tiny organism is only visible under a microscope, measuring about 0.1-0.2 millimeters across. Each cell is perfectly symmetrical, split into two halves with elaborate, branching lobes that radiate outward from the center. You'll find these beautiful geometric creatures floating in freshwater ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England.

idTips.label: Star-shaped symmetry
idTips.description: Under a microscope, the cell looks like a perfect six-pointed star with two identical halves divided by a narrow waist in the middle

idTips.label: Radiating lobes
idTips.description: Each half of the cell has three main lobes that branch and subdivide into smaller projections, creating an intricate lace-like pattern

idTips.label: Bright green color
idTips.description: The cell appears bright emerald green under the microscope due to its chloroplasts (the parts that do photosynthesis)

idTips.label: Smooth cell wall
idTips.description: The outer edge of the cell wall appears smooth and clean without spines or rough textures

idTips.label: Central constriction
idTips.description: A distinct narrow waist separates the two halves of the cell, making it look like a figure-eight from the side

habitat: Micrasterias radiosa lives in clean, soft-water environments like mountain ponds, bog pools, and quiet backwaters of streams. It prefers slightly acidic water with low mineral content, often found in the same habitats as sphagnum moss and other acid-loving plants. Look for it in the shallow, sunlit areas of these waters where it can photosynthesize effectively.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as water temperatures warm and daylight increases. This is often the best time to find them as they multiply rapidly in favorable conditions.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm summer months when photosynthesis is most active. Collect water samples from sunny, shallow areas for microscope viewing.
seasonality.fall: Numbers may decline as temperatures drop and daylight decreases, but cells can still be found in protected areas with stable temperatures.
seasonality.winter: Populations are at their lowest, though some cells may survive under ice in deeper water or as dormant stages.

funFact: Each Micrasterias cell is essentially a living work of art that takes about 24 hours to create its intricate, symmetrical pattern - and if you damage just one small part, the cell can regenerate that entire section perfectly!
confusionNotes: Micrasterias radiosa can be confused with other star-shaped desmid algae, but its specific pattern of three main lobes per half-cell with smooth margins helps distinguish it. Remember: 'radiosa' has rays that radiate smoothly outward, while other species may have more jagged or differently branched patterns.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'algae,' desmids like Micrasterias are actually more closely related to land plants than to seaweeds or pond scum. They're considered among the most beautiful microscopic organisms and are often used to assess water quality since they only thrive in clean, unpolluted environments.
compareHints: Micrasterias radiosa differs from its relatives by having smoother, more regularly branched lobes compared to the jagged edges of M. denticulata or the broader, flatter appearance of M. truncata. Its three-lobed pattern per half-cell is more symmetrical and delicate than the chunkier M. americana, and lacks the deep notches found in M. pinnatifida.
